Lec 6: Good and Bad Controls

library(rethinking)
library(dagitty)

Backdoor Criterion: Rule to find a set of variables to stratify by to yield \(P(Y|do(X))\)

  1. Identify all paths connecting the treatment X to the outcome Y
    1. The causes follow arrows but associations go both ways
  2. Paths with arrows entering X are backdoor paths (non-causal paths; confounding path)
    1. if you intervene on X, the change will not flow into backdoor path
    2. only arrows leaving X will be affected when changing X
  3. Find adjustment set that closes/blocks all backdoor paths

Example Flow

1) Identify all paths

  • \(X→ Y\)

  • \(X ← Z ← U → Y\)

2) Identify backdoor paths

  • \(X ← Z ← U → Y\) is a backdoor path

3) Minimal adjustment set

Block the pipe by stratifying by Z: X _ || _ U | Z

\[P(Y|do(X)) = \sum_z P(Y|X,Z) P(Z=z)\]

\[Y_i \sim {\sf Normal}(\mu_i,\sigma)\]

\[\mu_i = \alpha + \beta_XX_i + \beta_ZZ_i\]

# simulate confounded Y 
N <- 200 
b_XY <- 0 
b_UY <- -1
b_UZ <- -1
b_ZX <- 1 

set.seed(10)
U <- rbern(N)
Z <- rnorm(N, b_UZ*U)
X <- rnorm(N, b_ZX*Z)
Y <- rnorm(N, b_XY*X + b_UY*U)
d <- list(Y=Y, X=X, Z=Z)

# ignore U and Z (to compare first path vs second) 
m_YX <- quap(
  alist(
    Y ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + b_XY*X,
    a ~ dnorm(0,1),
    b_XY ~ dnorm(0,1),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=d
)

# Stratify by Z 
m_YXZ <- quap(
  alist(
    Y ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + b_XY*X +b_Z*Z,
    a ~ dnorm(0,1),
    b_XY ~ dnorm(0,1),
    b_Z ~ dnorm(0,1),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=d
)

post <- extract.samples(m_YX)
post2 <- extract.samples(m_YXZ)
dens(post$b_XY, lwd=3, col=1, xlab="posterior b_XY", xlim=c(-0.3,0.3))
dens(post2$b_XY, lwd=3, col=2, add=TRUE)
  • Remember, the true effect of X on Y is 0.
precis(m_YXZ)
             mean         sd        5.5%      94.5%
a     -0.32497443 0.09121807 -0.47075852 -0.1791903
b_XY  -0.01179336 0.07615873 -0.13350972  0.1099230
b_Z    0.24192499 0.11247432  0.06216931  0.4216807
sigma  1.17503769 0.05849399  1.08155299  1.2685224

  • in the model m_YXZ the coefficient for b_Z is meaningless (it does NOT mean that 0.24 is coefficient for Z on Y)

    • It’s a control variable - fallacy to intepret the coefficients of control variables!!

For any variable you add to the model as part of the adjustment set (in order to make it possible to get an estimate of some other variable’s coefficient) - usually its coefficients are not interpretable (Table 2 Fallacy)

More complicated example

1) List all the paths connecting X and Y. Which need to be closed to estimate the effect of X on Y?

\(X → Y\): direct causal path, necessarily open

Try to find mathematical way to delete the arrows that are entering X

  1. \(X ← C → Y\): non-causal, open
    1. Close by stratifying by \(C\) (add \(C\) to adjustment set)
  2. \(X ← Z → Y\): non-causal, open
    1. Close by stratifying by \(Z\); add \(Z\) to adjustment set
  3. \(X ← A → Z ← B → Y\): non-causal, closed (opened by stratifying on Z)
    1. Use A and/or B to close
  4. \(X ← A → Z → Y\): non-causal, open
    1. Already closed because we are stratifying by \(Z\)
  5. \(X ← Z ← B → Y\): non-causal, open
    1. Effectively closed because we are stratifying by \(Z\) (existing adjustment set)

Minimum adjustment set: C, Z, and either A or B. (B is better choice)

  • B is more statistically efficient than A

Example

G: grandparent education
P: parent education
C: child education
U: unobserved confound

1)

  1. \(G→ C\)
  2. \(G → P → C\): Pipe (P is a mediator)
  3. \(G → P ← U → C\): P is a collider

To find the direct causal effect of \(G\) on \(C\), we need to stratify by \(P\) (close the pipe). However, if we do that, then we open up Path 3 \(G → P ← U → C\), defined by the fork \(C← U → P\) (e.g., neighborhood variable). Can’t get the direct causal effect of G on C because we activate the confounds. It is possible to calculate the total effect of G on C, but that isn’t our research question.

Can estimate TOTAL effect of G on C Cannot estimate the DIRECT effect

\(C_i \sim {\sf Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)\)

\(\mu_i = \alpha + \beta_G G_i\)

\(C_i \sim {\sf Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)\)

\(\mu_i = \alpha + \beta_G G_i + \beta_PP_i\)
Confounded estimate, may end up concluding that G hurts C’s education

Controls

control variable: variable introduced to an analysis so that a causal estimate is possible

Wrong heuristics for choosing control variables:

  • anything goes

  • any variables not highly collinear

  • Any pre-treatment measurement (baseline)

  1. \(X → Y\) frontdoor and closed
  2. \(X ← u → Z ← v → Y\) backdoor and closed
    1. \(Z\) is collider
    2. Remains closed as long as we don’t condition on \(Z\)
    3. Not safe

X: win lottery
Y: Lifespan
Z: Happiness
u: contextual confounds

Conditioning on \(u\) is harmless UNLESS you try to stratify by \(Z\)! You can estimate the total causal effect of winning the lottery, but not direct causal effect.

  • Post-treatment variables are often risky controls

  1. \(X → Z → Y\)

  2. \(X → Z ← u → Y\)

    Note

    No backdoor path, no need to control for Z!!!

Simulate the DAG

Assume all arrows have effect of 1:

f <- function(n=100, bXZ=1, bZY=1){
  X <- rnorm(n)
  u <- rnorm(n)
  Z <- rnorm(n, bXZ*X + u)
  Y <- rnorm(n, bZY*Z + u)
  bX <- coef(lm(Y ~ X))['X']
  bXZ <- coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z))['X']
  return(c(bX,bXZ))
}

sim <- mcreplicate(1e4, f(), mc.cores = 8)

dens(sim[1,], lwd=3, xlab="posterior mean",xlim=c(-1,2), ylim=c(0,2.75))
dens(sim[2,], lwd=3, col=2, add=TRUE)

  • Adding Z in Y ~ X + Z makes it look like the effect is negative because it activates the confound

  • Y ~ X is correctly centered on 1.0

Now, assume all are 1 except bZY = 0 :

sim <- mcreplicate(1e4, f(bZY=0), mc.cores = 8)

dens(sim[1,], lwd=3, xlab="posterior mean",xlim=c(-1,0.5), ylim=c(0,3))
dens(sim[2,], lwd=3, col=2, add=TRUE)

  • Again, Y ~ X is correctly centered on 0 (\(X\) has no causal influence on \(Y\) )

  • While Y ~ X + Z mistakenly shows a negative relationship

Note

Statistical significance is not a guide to model structure.

Colliders

Note

Do not touch the collider! Colliders are BAD CONTROLS

Colliders are not always obvious:

  • Z becomes a collider if you consider the possibility of unmeasured causes between Z and Y

X: education
Y: income
Z: values
u: family

EX: How does education affect income? Imagine you have data on people’s values based on survey results, so you decide to condition on values (Z). But, you could be conditioning on a collider and accidentally get estimates that are higher SPURIOUS. Because values are often associated with family/upbringing (u), which can be associated with income (Y).

Non-backdoor examples

Case-control bias (selection on the outcome)

\[X (education) → Y (occupation) → Z (Income) \]

  • If you stratify based on income (Z), you’re weakly stratifying on the occupation Y, the outcome itself. It narrows the range of occupations that experiences a narrower range of education levels (false inferences)

Let’s see a simulation of this: (assume all arrows have coefficient of 1)

f <- function(n=100, bXY=1, bYZ=1){
  X <- rnorm(n)
  Y <- rnorm(n, bXY*X)
  Z <- rnorm(n, bYZ*Y)
  bX <- coef(lm(Y ~ X))['X']
  bXZ <- coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z))['X']
  return(c(bX,bXZ))
}

sim <- mcreplicate(1e4, f(), mc.cores = 8)

dens(sim[1,], lwd=3, xlab="posterior mean",xlim=c(0,1.5), ylim=c(0,5))
dens(sim[2,], lwd=3, col=2, add=TRUE)
  • Conditioning on \(Z\) gives a weaker association (by half)

Precision parasite

  • Stratifying on the parent of X

    \[Z → X → Y \]

Simulate the DAG

f <- function(n=100, bZX=1, bXY=1){
  Z <- rnorm(n)
  X <- rnorm(n, bZX*Z)
  Y <- rnorm(n, bXY*X)
  bX <- coef(lm(Y ~ X))['X']
  bXZ <- coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z))['X']
  return(c(bX,bXZ))
}

sim <- mcreplicate(1e4, f(), mc.cores = 8)

dens(sim[1,], lwd=3, xlab="posterior mean")
dens(sim[2,], lwd=3, col=2, add=TRUE)
  • Centers on the correct value, but it inflates the uncertainty (wider distribution)

Bias amplification

  • X and Y confounded by u

  • Something truly awful happens when we add Z

    • double activates the confound

X: occupation
Y: income
Z: education
u: regional/cultural factors

EX: Examining the association between occupation and income. Lots of regional and cultural factors that influences both. Stratifying by education seems reasonable… but this is a bias amplification problem.

Simulate: assume bXY is 0

f <- function(n=100, bZX=1, bXY=1){
  Z <- rnorm(n)
  u <- rnorm(n)
  X <- rnorm(n, bZX*Z + u)
  Y <- rnorm(n, bXY*X + u)
  bX <- coef(lm(Y ~ X))['X']
  bXZ <- coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z))['X']
  return(c(bX,bXZ))
}

sim <- mcreplicate(1e4, f(bXY=0), mc.cores = 8)

dens(sim[1,], lwd=3, xlab="posterior mean")
dens(sim[2,], lwd=3, col=2, add=TRUE)

  • Real value is 0 (no association between X and Y)… but the model finds association

  • The default model is already biased (we knew that - just the effect of an unobserved confound)

  • Conditioning on Z increases the bias

Why?

  • Covariation between X and Y can only exist if there’s variation in their causes

    • The cause of Y is X, and if X doesn’t vary then Y can’t vary

    • Then Z is a cause of X… so if Z doesn’t vary then X can’t vary

  • Within each level of Z, there is less variation in X

    • When we stratify by Z, we remove the variation in Z that causes X

    • Therefore the covariation between X and Y must be smaller within each level of Z

  • Consequently, confound \(u\) becomes relatively more important within each Z (when we condition on Z)

    • When you average across the levels of Z, you find more association between X and Y
n <- 1000 
Z <- rbern(n) # make Z binary to make viz of stratification easier (either 0 or 1)
u <- rnorm(n)
X <- rnorm(n, 7*Z + u)
Y <- rnorm(n, 0*X + u)

# looking for a slope of 0 = no association
Note

Control variable: variable introduced to an analysis so that a causal estimate is possible

Heuristics fail – adding control variables can be worse than omitting

Make assumptions explicit (must do scientific modeling [DAGs] to do scientific data analysis)
